english: it requires the proof that the sought function, which makes the integral a maximum or minimum, also possesses the higher derivatives.
topic: Hilbert finishes a proof that an approximating function must be divisible by x^2 and proposes generalizing the result to the calculus of variations, to show that the extremizing function possesses higher derivatives via uniform approximation by rational functions and partial integration.

triage.modern_statement: Here is the question in modern terms. Take a variational integral I[u] = ∫ F(x, u, ∇u) dx with a regular integrand, meaning F is smooth or analytic and strictly convex (elliptic) in the gradient. Suppose u minimizes or maximizes I but is only known to exist in a weak class, such as C^1 or a Sobolev space. Must u then have higher derivatives (C^2, C^∞, or even analytic) so that it solves the Euler–Lagrange equation classically? Hilbert's planned method was to approximate uniformly by rational functions and then integrate by parts. That method is specific to this diary entry, and I found no source that records it.
triage.answered_by: This entry is a precursor of Hilbert's 19th problem (Paris 1900), with the 20th problem closely related. The 19th asks whether solutions of regular variational problems are always analytic. S. N. Bernstein answered it for C^3 solutions in his 1904 thesis, starting with dimension n=2. E. De Giorgi (1956/57) and J. Nash (1957/58) then solved it independently in general by proving Hölder regularity for weak solutions. Earlier results then gave smoothness and analyticity. The resulting body of work is called De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 19th problem asks whether solutions of regular problems in the calculus of variations are always analytic. Bernstein answered it positively for C^3 solutions in 1904. De Giorgi and Nash solved it independently in the late 1950s.

Timeline: in 1904 Bernstein proved, in dimension n=2, that analyticity follows from C^3 regularity. In 1957 De Giorgi and Nash solved the problem independently. Together with Moser's work this became De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory, which was developed to settle the regularity of energy minimisers.
De Giorgi solved the 19th problem on regularity of solutions of elliptic PDEs in 1956/57, in parallel with John Nash.
The 19th problem asks whether minimizers of regular variational problems are necessarily analytic.

triage.why: The diary note asks for proof that the function extremizing a variational integral has higher derivatives. That is the regularity question Hilbert later published as Problem 19 (with Problem 20 related), so the subject matter matches closely. Bernstein, De Giorgi and Nash settled it for regular (elliptic) integrands. Regularity theory remains an active research area: a 2025 arXiv paper still builds on De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory, and work continues on non-divergence equations, degenerate cases and systems. I chose medium confidence for three reasons. First, the diary page is undated. Second, it may refer only to the one-variable case, where higher regularity of extremals follows from classical arguments. Third, no source I found discusses this specific notebook entry or its method of rational approximation and partial integration. The link to Problem 19 is my inference from the content, not something documented.
